title: Hello, Docker
summary: Check Docker is installed and run your very first container.

steps.text: Check that the Docker client and engine are both reachable.
steps.label: terminal

notes.text: "permission denied … docker.sock" means your user isn’t in the docker group. Run: sudo usermod -aG docker $USER, then log out and back in (or prefix commands with sudo for now).
"Cannot connect to the Docker daemon" means Docker Desktop isn’t running. Start it and wait for it to say it’s running.

steps.text: Run the hello-world image. Docker pulls it from Docker Hub, creates a container, runs it, and the container exits.
steps.label: terminal

steps.text: List the images now stored on your machine.
steps.label: terminal

expected: A "Hello from Docker!" message, and hello-world listed in docker images.

title: Run a web server
summary: Run nginx in the background, publish a port, read its logs, then stop and remove it.

steps.text: Start nginx detached (-d), name it "web", and map port 8080 on your machine to port 80 in the container.
steps.label: terminal

steps.text: Open http://localhost:8080 in your browser. You should see "Welcome to nginx!".
List running containers. Note the PORTS column.
steps.label: terminal

steps.text: Read the access log. Your browser request should be in it.
steps.label: terminal

steps.text: Stop and remove the container.
steps.code:
docker stop web
docker rm web
steps.label: terminal

expected: The nginx welcome page at localhost:8080, and a GET request line in docker logs.

title: Look inside a container
summary: Open a shell in a running container and change a file, then see the change disappear with the container.

steps.text: Start nginx again.
steps.label: terminal

steps.text: Open an interactive shell inside it.
steps.label: terminal

steps.text: Inside the container, overwrite the homepage, then leave the shell.
steps.code:
echo "

Edited from inside the container

" > /usr/share/nginx/html/index.html exit
steps.label: inside the container

steps.text: Refresh http://localhost:8080. Your edit is live.
Now remove the container and start a fresh one. Your edit is gone: container filesystems are disposable.
steps.code:
docker rm -f web
docker run -d --name web -p 8080:80 nginx:alpine
steps.label: terminal

steps.text: Clean up.
steps.label: terminal

expected: Your custom heading appears, then disappears after recreating the container.

title: Build your own image
summary: Write a Dockerfile, build an image from it, and run it.

steps.text: Go to your home folder, make a new folder, and move into it.
steps.label: terminal

steps.text: Create a file called index.html with this content.
steps.label: index.html

steps.text: Create a file called Dockerfile (no extension). Each instruction adds a layer on top of the base image.
steps.label: Dockerfile

notes.text: Notepad silently saves this as Dockerfile.txt and the build then fails. In the Save dialog choose "All files (*.*)", or use VS Code. Check with: dir

steps.text: Build it and tag it my-site:1.0. The "." is the build context: the current folder.
steps.label: terminal

steps.text: Run your image and open http://localhost:8081.
steps.label: terminal

steps.text: Change the heading in index.html, then rebuild as 1.1. Notice the FROM layer comes from cache. Only the COPY layer is rebuilt.
steps.code:
docker build -t my-site:1.1 .
docker rm -f my-site
docker run -d --name my-site -p 8081:80 my-site:1.1
steps.label: terminal

steps.text: Clean up the container (keep the images for now).
steps.label: terminal

expected: Your heading at localhost:8081, and both my-site:1.0 and my-site:1.1 in docker images.

files.note: Run every command from inside my-site.

title: Where the megabytes go
summary: Check how big an image is, read its layers with docker history, and see why deleting a file in a later step saves nothing.

steps.text: List your images and their sizes. Compare nginx:alpine with your own my-site images: yours are barely bigger, because they share the nginx layers.
steps.label: terminal

steps.text: Show the layers of your my-site image. Each Dockerfile step is one row, with the size it added. Your COPY step adds only a few bytes.
steps.label: terminal

steps.text: Go back to your home folder, make a new folder, and move into it.
steps.label: terminal

steps.text: Create a Dockerfile that makes a 50 MB file in one step and deletes it in the next.
steps.code:
FROM alpine:3.20
RUN dd if=/dev/zero of=/big.file bs=1M count=50
RUN rm /big.file
steps.label: Dockerfile

notes.text: Save it as Dockerfile, not Dockerfile.txt (choose "All files" in Notepad), or use VS Code.

steps.text: Build it, then check its size. It is about 60 MB, even though the file is gone.
steps.code:
docker build -t layers-demo:bloated .
docker image ls layers-demo
steps.label: terminal

steps.text: Look at the layers. The dd layer still holds 52 MB. Layers are read-only, so a later rm only hides the file: the bytes still ship.
steps.label: terminal

steps.text: Fix it: create and delete the file in the same RUN step, so the layer is saved without it.
steps.code:
FROM alpine:3.20
RUN dd if=/dev/zero of=/big.file bs=1M count=50 && rm /big.file
steps.label: Dockerfile

steps.text: Build the slim version and compare. In real Dockerfiles this is why you see `apk add --no-cache`, or `apt-get install` and `rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*` in one RUN.
steps.code:
docker build -t layers-demo:slim .
docker image ls layers-demo
steps.label: terminal

expected: layers-demo:bloated is about 60 MB and layers-demo:slim is about 9 MB, the same as alpine itself.

files.note: From step 3 on, run every command from inside layers-demo.

title: Cache your dependencies
summary: Order a Node.js Dockerfile so npm install only runs again when your dependencies change, not on every code change.

steps.text: Go back to your home folder, make a new folder, and move into it. You will use this small Node.js app for the next three exercises.
steps.label: terminal

steps.text: Create package.json. It lists one dependency (express) and one development-only tool (prettier).
steps.label: package.json

steps.text: Create greet.js.
steps.label: greet.js

steps.text: Create server.js. It answers every request with a JSON greeting.
steps.label: server.js

steps.text: Create a Dockerfile the simple way: copy everything, then install. You do not need Node.js on your machine: npm runs inside the build.
steps.code:
FROM node:24-alpine
WORKDIR /app
COPY . .
RUN npm install
CMD ["node", "server.js"]
steps.label: Dockerfile

notes.text: Save it as Dockerfile, not Dockerfile.txt (choose "All files" in Notepad), or use VS Code.

steps.text: Build it. The npm install step downloads about 70 packages.
steps.label: terminal

steps.text: Change "Hello" to "Hi" in greet.js, save, and build again. npm install runs again, although package.json did not change. COPY . . saw a changed file, so every step after it rebuilt.
steps.label: terminal

steps.text: Fix it: copy package.json on its own first, install, then copy the rest of the code.
steps.code:
FROM node:24-alpine
WORKDIR /app
COPY package.json ./
RUN npm install
COPY . .
CMD ["node", "server.js"]
steps.label: Dockerfile

steps.text: Build once (it installs again, because the steps changed). Then change "Hi" to "Hey" in greet.js and build again. This time npm install says CACHED and only the last COPY runs.
steps.code:
docker build -t node-app .
docker build -t node-app .
steps.label: terminal

steps.text: Run it and open http://localhost:8083. Then remove the container.
steps.code:
docker run -d --name node-app -p 8083:3000 node-app
docker rm -f node-app
steps.label: terminal

notes.text: Real projects also copy the lock file (package-lock.json) in that first COPY and use npm ci. PHP works the same way: copy composer.json and composer.lock, run composer install, then copy the code.

expected: After the fix, a code-only change rebuilds in about a second, with RUN npm install marked CACHED.

files.note: Run every command from inside node-app. There is no node_modules here: packages are installed inside the image.

title: Keep files out with .dockerignore
summary: COPY . . copies everything, secrets included. Use .dockerignore to decide what reaches the build.

steps.text: Stay in node-app. Create a .env file with a pretend secret, like many projects have.
steps.label: .env

notes.text: Save it as .env, not .env.txt (choose "All files" in Notepad), or use VS Code.

steps.text: Create a debug.log file too.
steps.label: debug.log

steps.text: Build and list the files inside the image. Your secret and your log file are both in there, for anyone who pulls the image.
steps.code:
docker build -t node-app .
docker run --rm node-app ls -a
steps.label: terminal

steps.text: Create a .dockerignore file. It works like .gitignore: matching files never reach the build. node_modules is there so a local install can never overwrite the one built in the image.
steps.label: .dockerignore

notes.text: Save it as .dockerignore, not .dockerignore.txt (choose "All files" in Notepad), or use VS Code.

steps.text: Build and list again. .env and debug.log are gone. The build output line "transferring context" also shows how much was sent to Docker.
steps.code:
docker build -t node-app .
docker run --rm node-app ls -a
steps.label: terminal

expected: The second listing has no .env and no debug.log.

title: Test and ship with multi-stage builds
summary: One Dockerfile, two targets: a test stage with every tool, and a lean production stage that runs as a normal user.

steps.text: Stay in node-app. Set greet.js back to "Hello", then add a test for it. node --test finds files ending in .test.js.
steps.label: greet.test.js

steps.text: Replace the Dockerfile with three stages. Each FROM starts a stage, and AS gives it a name. test and production both start from base.
steps.code:
FROM node:24-alpine AS base
WORKDIR /app
COPY package.json ./

FROM base AS test
RUN npm install
COPY . .
RUN npm test

FROM base AS production
ENV NODE_ENV=production
RUN npm install --omit=dev
COPY . .
USER node
CMD ["node", "server.js"]
steps.label: Dockerfile

steps.text: Build only the test stage with --target. The tests run during the build, and the build stops if any fail.
steps.label: terminal

steps.text: Break the test: change "Hello" to "Helo" in greet.js and build the test stage again. The build fails and shows expected and actual. Change it back afterwards.
steps.label: terminal

steps.text: Build the production image. With no --target, Docker builds the last stage, and skips stages it does not need, like test.
steps.label: terminal

steps.text: Compare them. production is smaller: --omit=dev left out prettier, and NODE_ENV=production tells libraries like express to run in production mode.
steps.code:
docker image ls node-app
docker run --rm node-app:test ls node_modules/prettier
docker run --rm node-app:prod ls node_modules/prettier
steps.label: terminal

steps.text: Run production and open http://localhost:8083. The response says "mode": "production". USER node means the app does not run as root.
steps.code:
docker run -d --name node-app -p 8083:3000 node-app:prod
docker exec node-app whoami
steps.label: terminal

steps.text: Remove the container. For a Laravel app the production stage runs composer install --no-dev --optimize-autoloader and php artisan optimize instead. This app's own api Dockerfile does exactly that, with a test stage that runs php artisan test.
steps.label: terminal

expected: The broken test fails the build, node-app:prod is smaller than node-app:test, has no prettier, and whoami prints node.

title: Scan an image for vulnerabilities
summary: Use Docker Scout, built into Docker Desktop, to find known security issues in your image and how to fix them.

steps.text: Scout needs a free Docker account. Sign in to Docker Desktop (top right), or run docker login in your terminal.
steps.label: terminal

notes.text: Docker Engine on its own does not include Scout. Use Docker Desktop for this exercise, or install the scout plugin from github.com/docker/scout-cli.

steps.text: In Docker Desktop, open Images and select node-app:prod. The Vulnerabilities view lists known issues (CVEs) by severity and which package each one is in.

The same from the terminal. quickview gives a summary and a health score: your USER node line already passes the non-root check. cves lists only the serious issues, and --locations shows the file each one was found in.
steps.code:
docker scout quickview node-app:prod
docker scout cves --only-severity critical,high --locations node-app:prod
steps.label: terminal

steps.text: Look at the paths: they are all under /usr/local/lib/node_modules/npm, which is npm itself, shipped in the node base image. Your code and express are clean. Ask Scout whether a newer or different base image would help.
steps.label: terminal

steps.text: For contrast, scan an old base image that no longer gets updates. It has dozens of high and critical issues and runs as root. The fix for most findings is a newer, smaller base image.
steps.label: terminal

expected: Your image shows a few high issues, all inside npm from the base image, while node:18-alpine shows dozens, including critical ones.

title: Keep data with volumes
summary: Use a named volume so data outlives the container that wrote it.

steps.text: Create a named volume.
steps.label: terminal

steps.text: Run a throwaway container (--rm deletes it on exit) that appends a line to a file in the volume. Run it twice. The single quotes matter: they stop your own shell from filling in $(hostname), so the container does it instead.
steps.code: docker run --rm -v notes:/data alpine sh -c 'echo hello from $(hostname) >> /data/notes.txt'
steps.label: terminal

steps.text: Read the file from yet another new container. Both lines are there, written by containers that no longer exist.
steps.label: terminal

steps.text: See where Docker keeps it.
steps.label: terminal

notes.text: The Mountpoint path is inside Docker Desktop’s Linux virtual machine, not on your own disk, so you won’t find it in Finder or Explorer.

expected: Two "hello from <id>" lines with different container ids.

title: Let containers talk
summary: Put two containers on a user-defined network and reach one from the other by name.

steps.text: Create a network.
steps.label: terminal

steps.text: Start Redis on that network, named "cache".
steps.label: terminal

steps.text: From a second container on the same network, ping Redis using just its name. Docker provides DNS for container names.
steps.code: docker run --rm --network dojo-net redis:7-alpine redis-cli -h cache ping
steps.label: terminal

steps.text: Try the same without the network flag. It fails: the default bridge network has no name resolution.
steps.code: docker run --rm redis:7-alpine redis-cli -h cache ping
steps.label: terminal

steps.text: Clean up.
steps.code:
docker rm -f cache
docker network rm dojo-net
steps.label: terminal

expected: PONG the first time, and a "Could not connect" / name error the second time.

title: Docker Compose: a two-service app
summary: Describe a database and an admin UI in one compose.yaml and start both with one command.

steps.text: Go back to your home folder, make a new folder, and move into it.
steps.label: terminal

steps.text: Create compose.yaml. Two services, one named volume, and depends_on to order startup. The services share a network automatically.
steps.code:
services:
  db:
    image: postgres:17-alpine
    environment:
      POSTGRES_USER: dojo
      POSTGRES_PASSWORD: dojo
      POSTGRES_DB: dojo
    volumes:
      - pgdata:/var/lib/postgresql/data

  adminer:
    image: adminer
    ports:
      - "8082:8080"
    depends_on:
      - db

volumes:
  pgdata:
steps.label: compose.yaml

steps.text: Start everything in the background.
steps.label: terminal

steps.text: Check status and follow the database log (Ctrl+C to stop following).
steps.code:
docker compose ps
docker compose logs -f db
steps.label: terminal

steps.text: Open http://localhost:8082 and log in: System "PostgreSQL", Server "db", Username "dojo", Password "dojo", Database "dojo". Create any table. The server name "db" works because Compose gives each service a DNS name.
Tear down and bring it back. Your table survives because it lives in the pgdata volume.
steps.code:
docker compose down
docker compose up -d
steps.label: terminal

steps.text: Now remove it all, including volumes (-v). This time the data is gone.
steps.label: terminal

expected: Adminer shows your table after down/up, and it is gone after down -v.

files.note: Run every command from inside compose-demo. Compose looks for compose.yaml in the current folder.

title: Read the Dojo’s own compose file
summary: This app is itself four containers. See how they are wired together.

steps.text: This is (a trimmed version of) the compose.yaml that runs the page you are reading.
steps.label: compose.yaml (excerpt)
steps.code:
services:
  db:
    image: mysql:8.4
    volumes: [dbdata:/var/lib/mysql]
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD", "mysqladmin", "ping", "-h", "127.0.0.1"]

  api:                           # Laravel on php-fpm
    build: ./apps/api            # built from a Dockerfile, not pulled
    image: docker-dojo-api
    environment:
      DB_HOST: db                # service name = hostname
    depends_on:
      db:
        condition: service_healthy   # wait until MySQL answers

  reverb:                        # websockets for the live tracker
    image: docker-dojo-api       # same image as api...
    command: ["php", "artisan", "reverb:start"]   # ...different command

  web:
    build: ./apps/web            # multi-stage: bun builds, nginx serves
    ports: ["8000:80"]           # the only port published to your machine

volumes:
  dbdata:

steps.text: Things to notice: only "web" publishes a port, so the database is unreachable from outside. "condition: service_healthy" makes the API wait until MySQL is ready, not just started. And one image serves two roles: the command decides whether it runs PHP-FPM or Reverb.
If your trainer shared the repository, run the whole Dojo yourself. --build builds the api and web images from source first.
steps.label: terminal
steps.code:
cd ~
git clone <repo-url-from-your-trainer> docker-dojo
cd docker-dojo
docker compose up -d --build

steps.text: Both Dojo images use multi-stage builds with a test stage. Run the API tests the same way you ran yours.
steps.code:
docker build --target test apps/api
docker build --target test apps/web
steps.label: terminal

steps.text: Open http://localhost:8000 to see your own copy. When you're finished, run: docker compose down

expected: You can explain why the database has no ports: entry, and what service_healthy does.

files.note: Only if you clone the repository in step 3. A trimmed view:

title: Clean up
summary: See how much space Docker is using and reclaim it.

steps.text: See disk usage by images, containers, volumes and build cache.
steps.label: terminal

steps.text: Remove what you made today. Removing a volume permanently deletes its data.
steps.code:
docker image rm my-site:1.0 my-site:1.1 layers-demo:bloated layers-demo:slim
docker image rm node-app node-app:test node-app:prod
docker volume rm notes
steps.label: terminal

steps.text: Optionally, remove all stopped containers and unused images in one go (asks for confirmation).
steps.label: terminal

steps.text: The builds left cached layers behind too. This clears the build cache.
steps.label: terminal

expected: docker system df reports less reclaimable space than before.
